key_concepts: [url]Rip verts and edges in Blender to make a vent^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8KOt9Imp_Zw[/url]
Use the Rip Tool to separate geometry.

content: Add a cube to the scene, scale it in the x- and z-axes, then [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale (Image 1). [k]Ctrl-R[/k] a Loop Cut down the middle (Image 2) and [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to bevel it (Image 3). Select the two edge loops (Image 4) and bevel them (Image 5). Add six Loop Cuts going the opposite direction (Image 6).

You can select an edge or vertex, press [k]V[/k], and that will rip it away from the other vertices it is connected to (Image 7). Whichever side your mouse is on when you press [k]V[/k] will indicate that the rip is occurring away from that side. Select several edges to rip (Image 8). [k]V,Z[/k] to rip and constrain it in the z-axis (Image 9). You will see that the rip created holes where backfaces are visible. One way to fix this would be to add a Solidify Modifier, but another option is to use [k]Alt-V[/k] which creates a face connection (Image 10).

key_concepts: [url]Creating an Ammo Crate for 3D printing - Full Workflow^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BAIqlKUta-U[/url]

content: Start with a cube, and [k]S,Y,1.5[/k], [k]S,Z,0.75[/k] to make a box that is 2m x 3m x 1.5m and [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale (Image 1).

image.caption: Image 1 - Starting with a cube, scaling it to make a box that is 2m x 3m x 1.5m and applying the scale

content: [k]Shift-D[/k] to duplicate the box. At this point, we need to make a decision. on the first box, select the side edges ([k]Shift-G,L[/k] will select all edges in the shape with the same length) (Image 2). Give the first box a wide bevel with six cuts, and the second box a narrow bevel with two cuts (Image 3). The first box with its wider, more rounded edges looks like its made of a formed polymer, while the second looks like welded or bent steel. For the futuristic look, we will go with the polymer style. Delete the second box and undo your changes on the first.

image.caption: Image 2 - Duplicating the box and selecting the side edges using Shift-G to select all edges of the same length
Image 3 - Giving the first box a wide bevel with six cuts for a polymer look and the second box a narrow bevel with two cuts for a welded steel look

content: Select all side edges and give it a deep bevel with one segment (Image 4). [k]Shift-G,L[/k] to select all side edges again and bevel those with six segments (Image 5). Select the bottom edge loop and bevel with six segments (Image 6).

image.caption: Image 4 - Selecting all side edges and giving it a deep bevel with one segment
Image 5 - Selecting all side edges again and beveling them with six segments
Image 6 - Selecting the bottom edge loop and beveling with six segments

content: Select the top face and [k]Shift-D,RMB,P,S[/k] to separate it as a new object (Image 7). In Edit Mode, [k]E,0.15[/k] to make it thicker (Image 8). In Object Mode, [k]S,Shift-Z[/k] to scale it out, but then make minor adjustments to make the thickness even in the x- and y-axes (Image 9).

image.caption: Image 7 - Selecting the top face and duplicating it in place and separating it as a new object
Image 8 - Going into Edit Mode and extruding to make it thicker
Image 9 - Going to Object Mode and scaling it out while making minor adjustments to keep the thickness even in the x- and y-axes

content: Go back to the main box, select the front face and [k]Shift-D,RMB,P,S[/k] to separate it as a new object (Image 10). [k]I[/k] to inset another face in the front face (Image 11). Select the outer vertices and [k]X,V[/k] to delete them and in Object Mode [k]G,X,Shift-drag[/k] to move the face out slightly in the x-axis to get rid of the z-fighting (Image 12).

image.caption: Image 10 - Going back to the main box, selecting the front face and duplicating it in place and separating it as a new object
Image 11 - Insetting another face in the front face
Image 12 - Selecting the outer vertices and deleting them and then moving the face out slightly in the x-axis in Object Mode to get rid of the z-fighting

content: With the face selected, [k]E,0.1,-[/k] to extrude the face inside the box (Image 13). In Object Mode, select the box and add a Boolean Modifier set to Difference with the front face as the Object (Image 14). If you hide the front face now, you will see that box now has an indentation on the front side where the front face was (Image 15). As long as we don't apply the modifier, wa can move the front face around and change the section being removed (Image 16). Get the front face object back to the center and flip any normals in that need it to fix the box (Image 17).

image.caption: Image 13 - Selecting the face and extruding it inside the box
Image 14 - Going to Object Mode, selecting the box and adding a Boolean Modifier set to Difference with the front face as the Object
Image 15 - Hiding the front face to reveal the indentation on the front side of the box where the front face was
Image 16 - Moving the front face around to show how the section being removed can be changed without applying the modifier
Image 17 - Getting the front face object back to the center and flipping any normals that need it to fix the box

content: Add a Loop Cut to the front face (Image 18). Delete the left-half and add a Mirror Modifier in the x-axis (Image 19). Hide the larger box (Image 20). Use the Knife Tool to cut an edge from the top corner to the bottom edge (Image 21). Bevel the edge (Image 22).

image.caption: Image 18 - Adding a Loop Cut to the front face
Image 19 - Deleting the left half and adding a Mirror Modifier in the x-axis
Image 20 - Hiding the larger box
Image 21 - Using the Knife Tool to cut an edge from the top corner to the bottom edge
Image 22 - Beveling the edge

content: You will need to fix the corner up top (Image 23). Extrude the vertices of the corner face in the x-, y-, and z-axes and delete the extra vertices (Image 24). Edge Slide the vertex in the corner out to close the face (Image 25). Extrude those face out in the y-axis (Image 26). Hide the front face, unhide the box and review the effect (Image 27).

image.caption: Image 23 - Fixing the corner up top
Image 24 - Extruding the vertices of the corner face in the x-, y-, and z-axes and deleting the extra vertices
Image 25 - Edge Sliding the vertex in the corner out to close the face
Image 26 - Extruding those faces out in the y-axis
Image 27 - Hiding the front face, unhiding the box and reviewing the effect

content: Hide the box again and go to work on the front face, deleting and creating faces so that in the end this is the shape we have (Image 28). Move around to the back of the front faces, set the Transform Pivot Point to Individual Origins and scale in the back faces (Image 29). Go into Vertex Select Mode and try to even out the depth on all sides (Image 30). Review the effect on the box (Image 31).

image.caption: Image 28 - Hiding the box and working on the front face, deleting and creating faces to achieve the desired shape
Image 29 - Moving to the back of the front faces, setting the Transform Pivot Point to Individual Origins and scaling in the back faces
Image 30 - Going into Vertex Select Mode and evening out the depth on all sides
Image 31 - Reviewing the effect on the box

content: We need to soften the sharp edges inside the depressions, so go around to the back, select the outer edges and [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to bevel them (Image 32). Review the effect on the box again (you can really see it in Material Preview Viewport Shading) (Image 33).

image.caption: Image 32 - Going around to the back, selecting the outer edges and beveling them to soften the sharp edges inside the depressions
Image 33 - Reviewing the effect on the box in Material Preview Viewport Shading

content: Select the top face of the top and [k]Shift-D,RMB,P,S[/k] to separate it as a new object (Image 34). Go to the new top object and [k]I[/k] to inset a face (Image 35). You will have some edges that create n-gons, go to the vertices at the corners, select a group, and [k]M,A[/k] to collapse them at the center (Image 36). Repeat this all around the inset face, and merge the final corner groups to make a rectangle, and delete the outer vertices (Image 37). Move the face up slightly in the z-axis to get rid of the z-fighting (Image 38).

image.caption: Image 34 - Selecting the top face of the top and duplicating it in place and separating it as a new object
Image 35 - Going to the new top object and insetting a face
Image 36 - Going to the vertices at the corners to fix n-gons, selecting a group and collapsing them at the center
Image 37 - Repeating this all around the inset face, merging the final corner groups to make a rectangle, and deleting the outer vertices
Image 38 - Moving the face up slightly in the z-axis to get rid of the z-fighting

content: [k]E,0.1,-1[/k] to move it down into the top (Image 39). In Object Mode, select the top and add a Boolean Modifier set to Difference with the top face as the Object (Image 40). Add two loop cuts to the top face to cut it into quarters, delete the opposite vertices, and add a Mirror Modifier in the x- and y-axes (Image 41). Move the left and top edges in to create a cross shape on top (Image 42).

image.caption: Image 39 - Extruding and moving it down into the top
Image 40 - Going to Object Mode, selecting the top and adding a Boolean Modifier set to Difference with the top face as the Object
Image 41 - Adding two loop cuts to the top face to cut it into quarters, deleting the opposite vertices, and adding a Mirror Modifier in the x- and y-axes
Image 42 - Moving the left and top edges in to create a cross shape on top

content: Fill in any missing faces (Image 43). Bevel the inner corner (Image 44). Move the middle edge inwards (Image 45). Scale in the back face and bevel the edges, like you did for the front face (Image 46).

image.caption: Image 43 - Filling in any missing faces
Image 44 - Beveling the inner corner
Image 45 - Moving the middle edge inwards
Image 46 - Scaling in the back face and beveling the edges as done for the front face

content: Duplicate and separate the side face as a new object, add a vertical Loop Cut, remove the left half, add a Mirror Modifier in the x-axis, inset a small face and move it towards the top (Image 47). Delete the outside vertices, move the face out in the x-axis to fix the z-fighting, extrude inwards, and add the Boolean Modifier to the box (Image 48). Inset a small face and extrude it in (Image 49). Cut an edge on the bottom face of the extrusion and [k]S,X,0[/k] to even it out (Image 50). Extrude the bottom face up, and now you have some handles (Image 51). Feel free to bevel the inside edges if you want.

image.caption: Image 47 - Duplicating and separating the side face as a new object, adding a vertical Loop Cut, removing the left half, adding a Mirror Modifier in the x-axis, insetting a small face and moving it towards the top
Image 48 - Deleting the outside vertices, moving the face out in the x-axis to fix the z-fighting, extruding inwards, and adding the Boolean Modifier to the box
Image 49 - Insetting a small face and extruding it in
Image 50 - Cutting an edge on the bottom face of the extrusion and evening it out in the x-axis
Image 51 - Extruding the bottom face up to create handles

key_concepts: [url]Using the Lattice Modifier - Creating an Axe in Blender^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x0pd6syEnJA[/url]
Making different shapes using the Lattice Modifier.

content: The Lattice Modifier is a deformation modifier available in Blender. It is non-destructive, so it doesn't alter the geometry of the mesh being modified until applied.

Start with the default cube, [k]Numpad3[/k] into Side View and [k]S,Shift-X[/k] to scale in the y- and z-axes, scale down in the y-axis, and then [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale (Image 1). Select the the two long edges on the side and [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to bevel them into the blade, leaving a small gap in the middle (Image 2). [k]G,Y[/k] to move the same edges back, making the blade sharper (Image 3). [k]1[/k] into vertex mode, select the two vertices near the blade and [k]J[/k] to join them, making the top face quads instead of an n-gon (Image 4). Repeat for the bottom face (Image 5).

image.caption: Image 1 - Starting with the default cube, going to Side View, scaling in the y- and z-axes, scaling down in the y-axis and applying the scale
Image 2 - Selecting the two long edges on the side and beveling them into the blade with a small gap in the middle
Image 3 - Moving the same edges back in the y-axis to make the blade sharper
Image 4 - Going into Vertex Mode, selecting the two vertices near the blade and joining them to make the top face quads instead of an n-gon
Image 5 - Repeating for the bottom face

content: [k]Shift-D,Y[/k] to duplicate the axe head and move it to the side (Image 6).

image.caption: Image 6 - Duplicating the axe head and moving it to the side

content: Move the 3D Cursor to the center of the axe blade you will be working in and [k]Shift-A > Lattice > Lattice[/k] (Image 7). The important thing with the lattice mesh is to remember to never apply the scale after transforming. Scale the lattice so that it is JUST larger than the axe head, making it a close fit (DO NOT APPLY SCALE) (Image 8). The lattice will allow us to deform the shape underneath it. We need to add edge loops to our lattice, and the way to do this is on the Data Properties tab. Under Lattice there is a Resolution section with values for U, V, and W. These correspond to the x-, y-, and z-axes. Increase the resolution in the W and you will see edge loops appear to segment the z-axis (Image 9). Before we can begin deforming the mesh, we need to add a Lattice Modifier to the axe head with the lattice as the target Object (Image 10). If we [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode with lattice, we see it has vertices we can manipulate. If we select some vertices move them out, we won't see the transformation affecting the axe head, even with the modifier in place (Image 11).

image.caption: Image 7 - Moving the 3D Cursor to the center of the axe blade and adding a Lattice to the scene
Image 8 - Scaling the lattice to be just larger than the axe head without applying the scale
Image 9 - Increasing the W Resolution in the Data Properties tab to add edge loops segmenting the z-axis
Image 10 - Adding a Lattice Modifier to the axe head with the lattice as the target Object
Image 11 - Going into Edit Mode with the lattice and seeing that moving vertices doesn't affect the axe head due to insufficient geometry

content: That's because the axe head doesn't have enough geometry; select the axe head and create several edge loops in the z-axis (Image 12). Now if we go back to the lattice and deform it, we will see the axe head deformed as well (Image 13). If you look, the deformation is limited by the lattice to stop after is reaches a vertex that is two stops away (Image 14). You will also notice the geometry in the back was pulled out as well. That is because the lattice only has a 2 in the V Resolution (Image 15). Increase the V Resolution, try again, and you will see that the influence stopped two vertices away (Image 16).

image.caption: Image 12 - Selecting the axe head and creating several edge loops in the z-axis
Image 13 - Going back to the lattice and deforming it to see the axe head deformed as well
Image 14 - Noticing the deformation is limited by the lattice to stop after reaching a vertex two stops away
Image 15 - Noticing the geometry in the back was pulled out as well because the lattice only has a V Resolution of 2
Image 16 - Increasing the V Resolution and seeing the influence stop two vertices away

content: Revert all your changes, [k]O[/k] to turn on Proportional Editing and change the Falloff to Sphere (Image 17). Drag the vertices out and you will get a rounded shape (Image 18).

image.caption: Image 17 - Reverting all changes, turning on Proportional Editing and changing the Falloff to Sphere
Image 18 - Dragging the vertices out to get a rounded shape

content: You could get the same results by using Proportional Editing directly on the object. The benefit of using the lattice is that it is non-destructive; if you go to edit your mesh it still has its original geometry (Image 19). Any changes made there will have the lattice applied to it. For example create an indentation in the middle of the blade (Image 20). With the lattice applied it bends the identation for you, which could have been difficult to do manually (Image 21).

image.caption: Image 19 - Showing the benefit of the lattice being non-destructive with the original mesh geometry preserved in Edit Mode
Image 20 - Creating an indentation in the middle of the blade
Image 21 - Seeing the lattice bend the indentation automatically

content: Select the vertex in the back and pull it out to make a spike (Image 22). Unfortunately, this also affected the indentation (Image 23). If we increase the W Resolution, we can move the bend further away so it doesn't affect the indentation (Image 24).

image.caption: Image 22 - Selecting the vertex in the back and pulling it out to make a spike
Image 23 - Noticing this also affected the indentation
Image 24 - Increasing the W Resolution to move the bend further away so it doesn't affect the indentation

content: Add a Cylinder to the scene, and scale it up in the z-axis, down in the x- and y-axes to make a handle (Image 25). Add several Loop Cuts in the z-axis (Image 26). Add a Lattice around the handle and increase the W Resolution (Image 27). Scale out the bottom vertices of the lattice (Image 28). Turn on [k]Proportional Editing > Smooth[/k] and [k]G,Y[/k] the bottom edge to add a slant to the handle (Image 29).

image.caption: Image 25 - Adding a Cylinder to the scene and scaling it up in the z-axis and down in the x- and y-axes to make a handle
Image 26 - Adding several Loop Cuts in the z-axis
Image 27 - Adding a Lattice around the handle and increasing the W Resolution
Image 28 - Scaling out the bottom vertices of the lattice
Image 29 - Turning on Proportional Editing set to Smooth and moving the bottom edge in the y-axis to add a slant to the handle

key_concepts: [url]Creating a Banner or Flag using Blender Physics Simulator^^https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Dl9dMRrHIc[/url]

content: Add a cube to the scene and [k]S,X[/k] to scale it out in the x-axis (Image 1). Add two Loop Cuts to cut it into quarters (Image 2). Remove the left and top halves and then add a Mirror Modifier in the x-a and y-axes (Image 3). Select the right edge, extrude it out and then scale it in the y-axis (Image 4).

image.caption: Image 1 - Adding a cube to the scene and scaling it out in the x-axis
Image 2 - Adding two Loop Cuts to cut it into quarters
Image 3 - Removing the left and top halves and adding a Mirror Modifier in the x- and y-axes
Image 4 - Selecting the right edge, extruding it out and then scaling it in the y-axis

content: Extrude the edge out further and add a Loop Cut in the middle (Image 5). Grab the top edge on the end and [k]G,Z[/k] to bring it up (Image 6). Select the inner edge loop and [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to bevel it with about 4-6 segments to smooth it out (Image 7). bevel the next edge loop with 6-8 segments and make it cover a wide area (Image 8).

image.caption: Image 5 - Extruding the edge out further and adding a Loop Cut in the middle
Image 6 - Grabbing the top edge on the end and moving it up
Image 7 - Selecting the inner edge loop and beveling it with about 4-6 segments to smooth it out
Image 8 - Beveling the next edge loop with 6-8 segments to cover a wide area

content: Select the top face and [k]I,B[/k] to inset a face while keeping the borders (Image 9). [k]G,G[/k] to Edge Slide the bottom vertex up to make a quarter-diamond face (Image 10). Select the diamond section and [k]E[/k] to extrude it up (Image 11). Extrude up once more to create a section for the sword tip (Image 12).

image.caption: Image 9 - Selecting the top face and insetting a face while keeping the borders
Image 10 - Edge Sliding the bottom vertex up to make a quarter-diamond face
Image 11 - Selecting the diamond section and extruding it up
Image 12 - Extruding up once more to create a section for the sword tip

content: Add several Loop Cuts to the tip section (Image 13). Turn on [k]Proportional Editing > Sharp[/k] (Image 14), select the top vertices and [k]S,Shift-Z[/k] to scale them in, making sure the Proportional Editor circle covers all vertices except the bottom (Image 15). Turn off Proportional Editing and select the top vertices and [k]M,A[/k] to merge them at center (Image 16).

image.caption: Image 13 - Adding several Loop Cuts to the tip section
Image 14 - Turning on Proportional Editing set to Sharp
Image 15 - Selecting the top vertices and scaling them in while making sure the Proportional Editor circle covers all vertices except the bottom
Image 16 - Turning off Proportional Editing, selecting the top vertices and merging them at center

content: A fuller is a rounded or beveled longitudinal groove or slot along the flat side of a blade (e.g., a sword, knife, or bayonet) that serves to both lighten and stiffen the blade, when considering its reduced weight. We will need to apply the Mirror Modifier before continuing (Image 17). We want the fuller to stop before the sword begins to curve, so add a Loop Cut to the blade somewhere below the curve (Image 18). Go down to the crossguard so you can see better, select the middle edges front and back, [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to bevel it to a width you like and then [k]P[/k] to adjust the profile shape to curve it (Image 19). This looks good until you get to the top. Select the vertices at the top on both sides and edge slide them up (Image 20). Select the edge loop going around the blade, [k]Ctrl-B,P[/k] to bevel it and adjust the profile to curve that section (Image 21).

image.caption: Image 17 - Applying the Mirror Modifier before adding the fuller
Image 18 - Adding a Loop Cut to the blade below the curve to mark where the fuller will stop
Image 19 - Selecting the middle edges front and back, beveling to a desired width and adjusting the profile shape to curve it
Image 20 - Selecting the vertices at the top on both sides and edge sliding them up
Image 21 - Selecting the edge loop going around the blade, beveling it and adjusting the profile to curve that section

content: Select the faces underneath the crossguard and subdivide them (Image 22). Select the inner faces and [k]F[/k] to turn them into one face (Image 23). [k]Mesh > Transform > To Sphere[/k] (or [k]Shift-Alt-S[/k]) and then move your mouse to change the face at the bottom into an oval shape (Image 24). Extrude the oval face down, inset, and extrude again (Image 25).

image.caption: Image 22 - Selecting the faces underneath the crossguard and subdividing them
Image 23 - Selecting the inner faces and turning them into one face
Image 24 - Using Mesh > Transform > To Sphere and moving the mouse to change the face at the bottom into an oval shape
Image 25 - Extruding the oval face down, insetting, and extruding again

content: Add a Loop Cut to the top section and [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to create some separation (Image 26). [k]Alt-E,F[/k] to create a gap (Image 27). Select the edges bevel them to make a nice rounded shape (Image 28).We want to round out the bottom face, so [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale and then [k]Shift-Alt-S[/k]) the bottom face into a circle shape (Image 29).

image.caption: Image 26 - Adding a Loop Cut to the top section and beveling it to create some separation
Image 27 - Extruding the faces along normals to create a gap
Image 28 - Selecting the edges and beveling them to make a nice rounded shape
Image 29 - Applying the scale and then using To Sphere to shape the bottom face into a circle

content: Add several Loop Cuts to the hilt (Image 30). Turn on [k]Proportional Editing > Smooth[/k], select the middle Loop Cut and  [k]S,Shift-Z[/k] widen the hilt (Image 31). Select the bottom face, extrude it down, select all side around the side and [k]Alt-E,F[/k] to extrude them out along normals (Image 32). Repeat the same steps as above to add a groove in the middle and bevel the outer edges (Image 33). for the pommels, select the bottom face again, extrude it out, and then widen the bottom (Image 34).

image.caption: Image 30 - Adding several Loop Cuts to the hilt
Image 31 - Turning on Proportional Editing set to Smooth, selecting the middle Loop Cut and widening the hilt
Image 32 - Selecting the bottom face, extruding it down, selecting all sides and extruding them out along normals
Image 33 - Repeating the same steps to add a groove in the middle and bevel the outer edges
Image 34 - Selecting the bottom face again, extruding it out and widening the bottom for the pommel

content: Select the bottom face of the pommel and inset it (Image 35). Select all edges around that inner face (Image 36). [k]RMB,S[/k] to subdivide them (Image 37).

image.caption: Image 35 - Selecting the bottom face of the pommel and insetting it
Image 36 - Selecting all edges around that inner face
Image 37 - Subdividing those edges

content: Turn on [k]Proportional Editing > Sphere[/k], select the inner face and [k]G,Z[/k] to bring it down in a rounded shape (Image 38). Round out the top of the pommel by adding a Loop Cut (image 39). Scale it in (Image 40). And Bevel it (image 41).

image.caption: Image 38 - Turning on Proportional Editing set to Sphere, selecting the inner face and bringing it down in a rounded shape
Image 39 - Rounding out the top of the pommel by adding a Loop Cut
Image 40 - Scaling it in
Image 41 - Beveling it

content: Select all edges you want to use for the wrapped handle and bevel them (Image 42). Select the top edge loops of all the bevels and [k]S,Shift-Z[/k] to bring them out (Image 43). [k]G,Z[/k] the edges down so they overlap the ones underneath (Image 44). Shift-Select the inner edge loops under the folds (Image 45). [k]Ctrl-Alt-Shift-S[/k] to use the [k]Shear Tool[/k] and [k]Y[/k] to limit it to the y-axis (Image 46).

image.caption: Image 42 - Selecting all edges to use for the wrapped handle and beveling them
Image 43 - Selecting the top edge loops of all the bevels and bringing them out
Image 44 - Moving the edges down so they overlap the ones underneath
Image 45 - Shift-selecting the inner edge loops under the folds
Image 46 - Using the Shear Tool and limiting it to the y-axis

compound_text: If you don't have it, install Extra Curve Objects (

content: The easiest way to start is to add a curve, so [k]Shift-A > Curve > Spirals > Archimedian[/k] (Image 1). The initial curve will resemble a circle (Image 2). If we adjust the Height, we will see the end of the curve rise up (Image 3). We can also change the rotation and affect the shape (Image 4). Adjusting the Radius Growth will adjust the curve; positive growth curves outwards, while negative growth curves in (Image 5).
Now that we have the path, we want to add thickness. Go to the Data Properties tab, and under [k]Geometry > Bevel[/k] adjust the depth and Fill Caps (Image 6).

section.header: Tapering the Horn with a Curve
content: Now we want to taper it, but we will use another curve for that. Add a Bezier Curve to the scene (Image 7). Go back to the spiral and under [k]Data Properties > Geometry[/k] set the bezier curve as the target of the Taper Object (Image 8).

The tapering is following the curve of the bezier; starting off at 0, increasing rapidly, followed by a return to 0 at the end (Image 9). If we [k]Tab[/k] into Edit Mode and move the end of the bezier curve up, we will see the spiral increase in thickness at the end (Image 10). What we want is a curve that starts of high and slopes downward (Image 11).

Let's say we want to change the spiral's body shape. We can introduce a new object to base our bevel on instead of round. [k]Shift-A > Curve > Circle[/k] (Image 12). Go back to the spiral and under [k]Data Properties > Geometry > Bevel[/k] set the type to Object and the Target Object to the new circle (Image 13). We ended up with almost the same shape we had before, but now we can modify it. Edit the circle's shape and you will see it reflected in the spiral (Image 14).

[k]Shift-D[/k] to duplicate the horn and the circle and move them out to get a better view (Image 15). Select the circle and [k]RMB > Convert > Mesh[/k] (Image 16). In Edit Mode select all vertices, [k]F[/k] to fill them in and [k]E[/k], [k]S[/k] to taper the shape (Image 17). [k]Ctrl-R[/k], [k]S[/k] to scale in the middle (Image 18). [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to bevel the middle (Image 19). And [k]Ctrl-B,C[/k] to bevel the bottom edge loop (Image 20). Add an Array Modifier in the z-axis, not going up less than 1.0 (Image 21). [k]O[/k] to turn on Proportional Editing, select the top edge loop and [k]S,Shift-Z[/k] to scale it out so it is interlocking with the top item (Image 22).

section.header: Transferring the Shape to the Curve
content: Select the curve and [k]Shift-S,T[/k] to move the 3D cursor there, and then select the shape and [k]Shift-S,E[/k] to move the shape to the cursor (Image 23). Add a Curve Modifier to the shape and set the spiral as its Curve Object (Image 24). If the shapes are pointing the wrong direction you can change the Deform Axis to a negative axis (Image 25). In the Array Modifier, update the Count to increase the number of segments (Image 26).

In the previous horn, the shape was applied to the curve, so when the curve was tapered, so was the shape. This time, the curve is applied to the shape; tapering the curve WILL NOT affect the shape. Instead, select the curve and in Edit Mode, [k]Alt-S[/k] to scale the vertices (make sure Proportional Editing is on) (Image 27). We want the scaling applied uniformly, so change the Falloff to Linear and enable Connected Only (Image 28). Now when you scale the end vertex, you will see a more uniform change applied, although you may need to increase the size of the proportional radius (Image 29). To increase the size of the horn, select the shape and [k]S[/k] to scale (Image 30).

content: Start with a Cylinder, however many vertices you like, and [k]S,Shift-Z[/k] to scale it in the x- and y-axes (Image 1). We want to make the pommel and crossguard so [k]Ctrl-R[/k] to add three Loop Cuts (Image 2). Select the face loops by the cuts and [k]Alt-E,F[/k] to extrude them out evenly (Image 3).

image.caption: Image 1 - Starting with a Cylinder and scaling it in the x- and y-axes
Image 2 - Adding three Loop Cuts to make the pommel and crossguard
Image 3 - Selecting the face loops by the cuts and extruding them out evenly

content: Add a cube, scale it down, and move it into position at the top of the shaft (Image 4). Select the two outside edges of the cube (Image 5). [k]RMB,S[/k] to subdivide it with three cuts (Image 6). Select the edge second from the top and [k]G,G[/k] to slide it up (Image 7).

image.caption: Image 4 - Adding a cube, scaling it down and moving it into position at the top of the shaft
Image 5 - Selecting the two outside edges of the cube
Image 6 - Subdividing it with three cuts
Image 7 - Selecting the edge second from the top and sliding it up

content: Select the top edge and slide it back (Image 8). We want to move the bottom face back as well, but keep it lined up with the top, so select the bottom face and [k]G[/k] to move it, [k]B[/k] to activate Snap Base and choose the top edge (Image 9). This will restrict movement so that you can align with the top. Select the two edges on the outside of the bottom face and [k]RMB,S[/k] to subdivide it (Image 10). Slide the bottom edge in to make a sort of butterfly shape (Image 11).

image.caption: Image 8 - Selecting the top edge and sliding it back
Image 9 - Selecting the bottom face and moving it while activating Snap Base to the top edge to keep it aligned
Image 10 - Selecting the two edges on the outside of the bottom face and subdividing them
Image 11 - Sliding the bottom edge in to make a sort of butterfly shape

content: [k]Tab[/k] into Object Mode and [k]Ctrl-A,S[/k] to apply the scale, if you don't the bevel won't apply evenly (Image 12). Select the outside edges (Image 13). [k]Ctrl-B[/k] to bevel them, but not all the way since this is an energy weapon, not a weapon designed to penetrate armour (Image 14).

image.caption: Image 12 - Going to Object Mode and applying the scale so the bevel will apply evenly
Image 13 - Selecting the outside edges
Image 14 - Beveling them, but not all the way since this is an energy weapon

content: Change the Transform Pivot Point to 3D Cursor (Image 15), and [k]Alt-D,R,90[/k] to create four linked duplicates rotated around the haft (Image 16). Make any adjustments to the flange's geometry in Edit Mode, and it will be applied to all (Image 17).

image.caption: Image 15 - Changing the Transform Pivot Point to 3D Cursor
Image 16 - Creating four linked duplicates rotated around the haft
Image 17 - Making adjustments to the flange's geometry in Edit Mode and seeing them applied to all linked duplicates

content: Add a new Cylinder, and scale it down so it covers the top part of the haft, give it a rotation and apply ([k]Ctrl-A,R[/k] (Image 18). Add a Cube to the scene, scale and mirror so it covers part of the new cylinder evenly on two sides (Image 19). Go into Local View with the cube ([k]/[/k]) and update the shape using [k]G[/k], [k]Ctrl-B[/k] (Image 20). Add a Boolean Modifier to the cylinder with the cube as the target object (Image 21). Apply the modifier to the cube and move one side down to create some difference (Image 22).

image.caption: Image 18 - Adding a new Cylinder, scaling it down to cover the top part of the haft, giving it a rotation and applying it
Image 19 - Adding a Cube to the scene, scaling and mirroring it to cover part of the new cylinder evenly on two sides
Image 20 - Going into Local View with the cube and updating the shape using moving and beveling
Image 21 - Adding a Boolean Modifier to the cylinder with the cube as the target object
Image 22 - Applying the modifier to the cube and moving one side down to create some difference

content: Change the Transform Pivot Point back to the 3D Cursor, select a flange and [k]Alt-D,R,45[/k] (Image 23). Add three more (Image 24). The flanges are running over each other, so select one, and in Edit Mode scale in the thickness (Image 25). Select the four corner flanges, set the Transform Pivot Point to Individual Origins and scale them in Edit Mode to make them smaller (Image 26).

image.caption: Image 23 - Changing the Transform Pivot Point back to the 3D Cursor, selecting a flange and creating a linked duplicate rotated 45 degrees
Image 24 - Adding three more flanges
Image 25 - Selecting one flange and scaling in the thickness in Edit Mode to fix the overlapping
Image 26 - Selecting the four corner flanges, setting the Transform Pivot Point to Individual Origins and scaling them down in Edit Mode to make them smaller

content: Add a Cube to the side with the longer covering and scale it down (Image 27). Apply the scale and bevel the bottom edge (Image 28). Bevel the edges on the sides (Image 29).

image.caption: Image 27 - Adding a Cube to the side with the longer covering and scaling it down
Image 28 - Applying the scale and beveling the bottom edge
Image 29 - Beveling the edges on the sides

content: Add a new Cube and scale it down so it is a thin cube embedded in the power unit (Image 30). Go into Local View and [k]B,C[/k] to bevel the bottom edges and clamp it, creating a rounded end (Image 31). Exit Local View and add an Array Modifier in the z-axis (Image 32). [k]Shift-D[/k] to duplicate the power unit, and leave it in place (Image 33). Add a Boolean Modifier to the power unit with the rounded-end wedges as the target; hide the rounded-end wedges (Image 34).

image.caption: Image 30 - Adding a new Cube and scaling it down so it is a thin cube embedded in the power unit
Image 31 - Going into Local View and beveling the bottom edges with clamping to create a rounded end
Image 32 - Exiting Local View and adding an Array Modifier in the z-axis
Image 33 - Duplicating the power unit and leaving it in place
Image 34 - Adding a Boolean Modifier to the power unit with the rounded-end wedges as the target and hiding the rounded-end wedges

content: Select the duplicate power unit and scale it down (Image 35). We want a separator for our vents, so go back to the wedge mesh, and add a Loop Cut down the middle (Image 36). Bevel the edge loop until you reach the desired thickness, delete the faces and fill in the gaps (Image 37). Hide the wedges again (Image 38). Select the inner mesh, cutting round wedges, and parent the outer power unit to them, so that if you move the power unit, the other pieces come with it (Image 39).

image.caption: Image 35 - Selecting the duplicate power unit and scaling it down
Image 36 - Going back to the wedge mesh and adding a Loop Cut down the middle to create a separator for the vents
Image 37 - Beveling the edge loop until reaching the desired thickness, deleting the faces and filling in the gaps
Image 38 - Hiding the wedges again
Image 39 - Selecting the inner mesh cutting round wedges and parenting the outer power unit to them so that moving the power unit brings the other pieces along

content: Add several Loop Cuts to the grip (Image 40). Select all faces in the grip, and [k]I,I[/k] to inset faces individually (Image 41). Inset the faces again, but this time use [k]Ctrl[/k] to affect the depth (Image 42).

image.caption: Image 40 - Adding several Loop Cuts to the grip
Image 41 - Selecting all faces in the grip and insetting faces individually
Image 42 - Insetting the faces again using Ctrl to affect the depth

content: Select a face along the bottom of the grip and [k]Shift-S,T[/k] to position the 3D Cursor (Image 43). Add an Ico Sphere to the scene and scale it down (Image 44). [k]Shift-S,W[/k] to move the 3D Cursor back to the World Origin, set the Transform Pivot Point to 3D Cursor, and [k]Alt-D,R,90[/k] to make four studs around the bottom (Image 45). Repeat these steps at the top of the grip (Image 46). Add two more studs up by the power unit (Image 47).

image.caption: Image 43 - Selecting a face along the bottom of the grip and positioning the 3D Cursor there
Image 44 - Adding an Ico Sphere to the scene and scaling it down
Image 45 - Moving the 3D Cursor back to the World Origin, setting the Transform Pivot Point to 3D Cursor and making four studs around the bottom
Image 46 - Repeating these steps at the top of the grip
Image 47 - Adding two more studs up by the power unit
Image 48 - Final Render
